# Two captured vertices: an all-dimensional section-product theorem

Let T be a d-simplex, d>=2, and let a proper oriented hyperplane section
have exactly two strictly captured vertices. Give their affine heights
the names p>=q>0. Every other height is nonpositive, and at least one is
strictly negative. Let b be the barycentric centroid of the section and
F the fraction of T on the captured closed side.

**Theorem.** If the centroid coordinate at the q-vertex is at most 1/d,
then

    F > d^d product_(j different from the p-vertex) b_j.     (1)

Equal positive heights are permitted. Repeated negative heights and
zero-height vertices are also permitted. No restriction on the other
centroid coordinates is needed for (1).

The argument uses the complete scalar theorem in
`candidate 5f357f58008cdf1e`.
The equal-height case is supplied by
`candidate 4ac6f62135b1565c`, with
the explicit zero-height reduction below. These are proved dependencies,
not unproved allocation or localization hypotheses.

## 1. Exact derivatives and the section centroid

Write a uniform barycentric point as U_j=E_j/G, where the E_j are
independent unit exponentials and G=sum E_j. The change of variables
has Jacobian G^d, so U is uniform and independent of the gamma variable
G. The captured event is V=sum c_j E_j>=0, with c the vertex heights.

Let f_V(0)>0 be the density of V at zero, and let P_j denote the
derivative of its captured probability with respect to height c_j.
Then

    P_j=d f_V(0) b_j.                                  (2)

Indeed, differentiating the simplex halfspace integral gives
P_j=f_L(0)b_j for L=sum c_j U_j. The derivative follows by slicing along
the cut normal; its difference quotient is bounded on a fixed compact
projection, and the boundary of the proper section has relative measure
zero. Thus vertex incidences cause no exception. Independence of G and U
gives f_V(0)=f_L(0)E[1/G]=f_L(0)/d. This proves (2).

In this note the section is proper and crosses the simplex interior.
The sum of two positive exponential phases and at least one negative
phase has a bounded continuous density, positive at zero; this also
justifies the exponential differentiations below directly. Each density
and derivative formula remains regular when negative heights coincide.

## 2. Unequal positive heights

First omit zero heights, and write the strictly negative heights as
-r_j with r_j>0, j=1,...,m. There is no requirement that the r_j be
distinct. Assume p>q. Put

    s_j=p/(p+r_j), t_j=q/(q+r_j),
    X=product s_j, Y=product t_j, rho=Y/X,
    h=1-q/p, a_j=r_j/(q+r_j), S=sum a_j,
    L=h rho/(1-rho).

All s_j,t_j,a_j,rho lie strictly between zero and one; 0<h<1.
The positive sum pE_0+qE_1 has density

    [exp(-u/p)-exp(-u/q)]/(p-q),  u>0,

and survival function

    [p exp(-u/p)-q exp(-u/q)]/(p-q).

Conditioning on W=sum r_j E_(j+1) and using its product Laplace transform
therefore gives the exact formulas

    F=(pX-qY)/(p-q),
    f_V(0)=(X-Y)/(p-q).                                (3)

Differentiate (3) in q, and differentiate it negatively in each r_j.
After dividing by f_V(0), relation (2) gives

    d b_q = 1/h-rho S/(1-rho)=(1-LS)/h,

    d b_(negative j)
        =(s_j-rho t_j)/(1-rho)=s_j(1+L a_j).            (4)

Here the elementary identities

    t_j/s_j=1-h a_j,
    rho=product_j(1-h a_j)

explain all factors in (4). In particular, the assumed centrality at
the q-vertex is exactly

    LS>=1-h.                                          (5)

The right side of (1), divided by X, is

    [(1-LS)/h] product_j(1+L a_j).

The left side divided by X is `[1-(1-h)rho]/h`.
The universal product theorem, applied to x_j=h a_j, gives

    (1-LS) product_j(1+L a_j)
        <=1-rho LS <=1-(1-h)rho,                       (6)

where the second inequality is exactly (5). This proves (1) without
approximating either the cap or its selected vertex.

If m>=2, the first inequality in (6) is strict. If m=1, its equality
case causes no loss: then LS=1-h a_1>1-h because a_1<1, so the second
inequality is strict. Thus (1) is strict in every proper unequal case.

## 3. Equal heights and zero-height vertices

When p=q, scale both to one. The exact equal-height theorem cited above
proves (1), strictly, with no unequal-height limiting argument. In that
calculation the two captured centroid coordinates are equal, so either
captured vertex can be designated as r.

Zero-height vertices can be removed explicitly from the exponential
calculation. Their independent exponential variables do not appear in V.
For such an index j, changing its zero coefficient by epsilon gives

    d/d epsilon Pr(V+epsilon E_j>=0)|_(epsilon=0)
        =f_V(0) E E_j=f_V(0).

The bounded continuous density of V and integrability of E_j justify
dominated differentiation from either sign. Equation (2) consequently
gives d b_j=1. Each zero-height vertex contributes exactly a factor one
to the product of the quantities d b_j.

After omitting z zero phases, the remaining problem has effective
simplex dimension m+1. The quantities P_j/f_V(0) are unchanged, so they
equal both d b_j in the original section and `(m+1)b_j^eff` in the
effective section. Centrality at the q-vertex is the same inequality
P_q/f_V(0)<=1. The unequal or equal-height argument in that effective
dimension therefore gives precisely (1) in the original dimension.
This is an identity-based reduction, not an exchange of potentially
singular limits.

## 4. Optional strengthening to both captured vertices

The same hypothesis also implies the product bound with the q-vertex
omitted. Here is the explicit additional dependency. The reciprocal
Laplace-transform lemma proved in Sections 1--3 of
`candidate 8704554a92158bfc` states the following.
For the current log-concave density f_V, put

    phi(c)=f_(V+cE')(0)/f_V(0),   psi(c)=1/phi(c), c>0.

Then psi is convex, psi(0+)=1, and psi(c)>=1 implies psi'(c)>0.
Size bias gives phi(p)=d b_p and phi(q)=d b_q. Our centrality assumption
means psi(q)>=1. Convexity and the positive derivative from q onward
give phi(p)<=phi(q), that is b_p<=b_q. Therefore the product excluding
q is at most the product excluding p. The strict bound (1) proves the
former as well. For p=q this follows directly by symmetry.

This optional corollary uses the already proved reciprocal-transform
lemma. It does not assume that section-centroid stationarity persists
under a finite cap deformation.

## Scope

The theorem proves the requested specified-cap product comparison for
all dimensions when exactly two vertices have strictly positive raw
height, including through-vertex cuts. It does not cover three or more
strictly positive and two or more strictly negative heights. Nor does it
promote an ordinary simplex statement to arbitrary convex bodies,
mixed-integer fibers, or a complete proof of OC.
